title: Counting by night
hook: during the Omer, the day's count is said at evening prayer

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hashkiveinu, lay us down in peace. Your line was spread the shelter. Whose night did you look after? Tonight, something extra that the evening service holds for seven weeks a year. Day six hundred twelve.

Days till vacation. Sleeps till a birthday. Weeks till a baby is due. A countdown makes waiting feel like it's going somewhere. For seven weeks every spring, from the second night of Passover until Shavuot, Jewish tradition keeps a different kind of count, out loud, one day at a time. Not with an app. At the end of the evening service, the congregation stops, says a blessing, and announces the number. Today is twelve days, which is one week and five days. And then they go home. Tomorrow night, thirteen.
screen: `COUNTING DOWN TO THINGS.` → `SEVEN WEEKS EVERY SPRING.` → `TODAY IS TWELVE DAYS.`

segments.voice: The count comes from Leviticus. In the old Jewish translation: "And ye shall count unto you from the morrow after the day of rest, from the day that ye brought the sheaf of the waving; seven weeks shall there be complete." The sheaf is the omer, a measure of new barley brought to the Temple on the second day of Passover. So the count is called sefirat ha'omer, counting the omer. Forty-nine days, and on the fiftieth, Shavuot, the festival of the wheat harvest and, in Jewish tradition, of receiving the Torah at Sinai. Why count at night? Because in the Jewish calendar, a day begins at sundown. And the verse says the weeks should be complete, temimot. If you counted in the morning, you'd miss part of the day. Counting at nightfall catches each day from its very start. So it belongs to Maariv. The count has a rule that makes people careful. If you forget to count one night, you can still count the next day, without the blessing. But if you miss a whole day, many authorities say you keep counting for the rest of the weeks without saying the blessing. The chain matters. Notice what kind of counting it is. Not down, but up. Not days left until Shavuot, but days already lived since Passover. From freedom toward the Torah, step by step. Each number is a small claim: I was here for this one too.
screen: `SEVEN WEEKS SHALL THERE BE COMPLETE.` · `THE OMER: A SHEAF OF BARLEY.` · `A DAY BEGINS AT SUNDOWN.` · `COUNTING UP, NOT DOWN.` · then, large: `COUNT BY NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: count something tonight. Settle, and breathe. Choose one thing you're in the middle of. Days since you started something. Weeks you've kept a habit. Days on this path. Count it up, not down. Say the number out loud, the way the omer is said: today is this many days. Then breathe, and let the number mean something. Each one was a day you showed up. The bell holds the time.
Counting by night. Sefirat ha'omer, the forty-nine days from Passover to Shavuot, counted up at evening prayer.
Your line: count by night. Tonight, before you sleep, say one number out loud: how many days you've kept something going. Day six hundred twelve.

howItsDone: From the second night of Passover until the night before Shavuot, the omer is counted each night after nightfall, usually at the end of Maariv: a blessing, then the day's number in days and weeks. Someone who misses a full day continues counting without the blessing, according to common practice.

trapdoor: what you thought: a countdown calendar to a holiday.
what it means: counting up, night by night, from freedom at Passover to the Torah at Shavuot.
what a scholar hears: Leviticus 23:15's temimot, complete, is why the count starts at nightfall and why many hold that a missed day ends the blessing.

sources.quoted: And ye shall count unto you from the morrow after the day of rest, from the day that ye brought the sheaf of the waving; seven weeks shall there be complete

notes: Leviticus 23:15 quoted from JPS 1917 from memory; verify ('day of rest', 'sheaf of the waving').
Counting at night because of temimot: Menachot 66a / Tosafot; confirm citation.
Missing a whole day: Shulchan Aruch OC 489:8 (continue without blessing); confirm.
The rabbinic reading of 'the morrow after the day of rest' as the day after the first day of Passover is taken for granted; other ancient readings are not discussed.
Shavuot as the time of the giving of the Torah is rabbinic tradition, said so.

Editor review (y2 595–612): light polish only. The hook no longer tells the listener what they've done ('You've counted down to things') or says flatly that 'Jews count'; it now says Jewish tradition keeps the count. Teach, games and halachic details unchanged.
